name: Mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration
aliases: neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 4

reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: A form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) caused by variants in C19orf12, most often autosomal recessive but occasionally dominant
Typically presents in childhood or early adulthood with progressive spastic paraparesis, dystonia, parkinsonism, and motor axonal neuropathy
Optic atrophy and progressive cognitive decline with neuropsychiatric features are characteristic
Brain MRI shows iron deposition (T2 hypointensity) in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, sometimes with a hyperintense streak in the medial medullary lamina
Neuropathology demonstrates iron accumulation, Lewy-body-like alpha-synuclein pathology, and axonal spheroids
C19orf12 encodes a small mitochondrial membrane protein implicated in lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function
The combination of pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and lower-motor-neuron signs with optic atrophy is a useful diagnostic clue
No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive, with management of dystonia, spasticity, and neuropsychiatric symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: MPAN belongs to the NBIA group and is caused by variants in C19orf12, which encodes a small protein localised to mitochondrial membranes and implicated in lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial function. Loss of normal protein function disturbs mitochondrial and lipid metabolism in vulnerable neurons, leading to progressive neurodegeneration accompanied by pathological iron deposition in the basal ganglia, particularly the globus pallidus and substantia nigra. The neuropathology characteristically shows axonal spheroids and alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy-body-like inclusions in addition to iron, linking the disorder to both iron-accumulation and synucleinopathy mechanisms. This produces the mixed clinical picture of upper motor neuron, extrapyramidal, and peripheral nerve involvement with optic atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Other NBIA disorders (PKAN, PLAN, BPAN, and related conditions)
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies with central features
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences of the basal ganglia
C19orf12 molecular genetic testing (often within an NBIA gene panel)
Nerve conduction studies for motor axonal neuropathy
Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies to exclude Wilson disease
redFlags: Rapid loss of ambulation from progressive spasticity and dystonia
Severe dystonic crisis requiring urgent management
Marked neuropsychiatric deterioration with safety concerns
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy
reference.prognosis: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder leading to increasing motor and cognitive disability over years to decades; no treatment halts progression and care is supportive.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the diagnostic MRI iron pattern and pursuing broader neurology unnecessarily
Attributing the peripheral neuropathy to a separate cause rather than the same disorder
Overlooking the neuropsychiatric component of the phenotype
Not excluding treatable mimics such as Wilson disease before settling on the diagnosis
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: No disease-modifying treatment for this C19orf12-related NBIA; care is supportive and symptom-directed
Treat dystonia with anticholinergics, baclofen or botulinum toxin injections, reserving deep brain stimulation for refractory disabling dystonia
Manage spasticity and parkinsonism with antispasticity agents, physiotherapy and a levodopa trial, and support the motor axonal neuropathy with orthoses and mobility aids
Psychiatric and cognitive management of the neuropsychiatric features and progressive dementia
Low-vision rehabilitation and ophthalmology follow-up for the progressive optic atrophy
Multidisciplinary neurology-led care with speech and language therapy, dietetic and swallowing support, and palliative planning as disability progresses
Autosomal recessive (occasionally dominant) genetic counselling and cascade family testing for C19orf12 variants
